topics.t: Thirupparankundram hill and the Karthigai Deepam
topics.news: Tamil Nadu asked the Supreme Court to stay the Madras High Court’s January order that lets the temple’s management light the Karthigai Deepam on a stone pillar (the Deepathoon) on Thirupparankundram hill. The State says the pillar stands next to a dargah and the move could disturb public peace, so the position on the ground must stay as it is until its appeal is decided. The High Court had called the fear an ‘imaginary ghost’. A Bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi heard the case on Tuesday and will continue on Wednesday.

rows: Freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to **public order, morality and health** and the other Fundamental Rights. Art. 25(2) lets the State regulate secular activity linked to religion and throw open Hindu temples to all classes.
Every religious denomination can manage its own affairs in matters of religion and own and administer property **in accordance with law** (again subject to public order, morality and health).

Courts protect only practices that are essential to a religion. The test began with the **Shirur Mutt case (1954)** and was applied in many later cases. A nine-judge Bench was set up after the Sabarimala review (2019) to settle how far courts may decide what is essential.

A ground on which Arts. 25 and 26 can be limited. The State may regulate the time, place and manner of a festival if there is a real risk to peace, but the fear has to rest on material and not on speculation.
A court order that freezes the position on the ground until the case is decided. It is asked for when a step cannot be undone, such as lighting a lamp at a disputed spot.

The **Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959** lets the State’s HR&CE Department administer most large Hindu temples. The Supreme Court in **Dr Subramanian Swamy v. State of Tamil Nadu (2014)** held that the Chidambaram Nataraja temple belonged to its denomination of priests and set aside State control.
Keeps the religious character of a place of worship as it stood on 15 August 1947 (the Ayodhya site was excluded). It is part of the background to disputes next to places of worship of another faith.

ul: **The temple:** Thirupparankundram, near Madurai, is the first of the six abodes of Murugan (Arupadai Veedu). The others are Tiruchendur, Palani, Swamimalai, Thiruthani and Pazhamudircholai.

**The festival:** Karthigai Deepam falls on the full-moon day of the Tamil month Karthigai (November–December), when the Krittika star rules the sky. The great lamp on the Annamalai hill at Tiruvannamalai is the best known.

**The two questions before the Court:** whether there is an established custom of lighting the lamp on the pillar (a question of evidence, with the State saying it has been lit only at the Deepa Mandapam for over 150 years) and whether the fear of disorder is serious enough to restrict the right.

prel.d: Freedom of conscience and free practice of religion, subject to public order, morality and health and to other Fundamental Rights.
The right of religious denominations to manage their own religious affairs and to own and administer property in accordance with law.
The judicial test that protects only those practices that are essential to a religion; first used in the Shirur Mutt case (1954).
An order that keeps things as they are on the ground until the main case is decided.
A ground in Arts. 19, 25 and 26 for restricting rights; it concerns disturbance of peace that affects the community at large.
The State department that administers Hindu religious and charitable endowments under the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959.
The six abodes of Lord Murugan in Tamil Nadu: Thirupparankundram, Tiruchendur, Palani, Swamimalai, Thiruthani and Pazhamudircholai.
The Tamil festival of lights on the full moon of Karthigai month, when large lamps are lit on hills and in temples.
Freezes the religious character of places of worship as on 15 August 1947, except the Ayodhya site.

qs.q: Freedom of religion under Articles 25 and 26 is not absolute. Discuss how courts have balanced religious custom with public order, with recent examples.
qs.ref: 2024 GS2 (India as a secular state) · 2022 GS1 (Indian secularism)

qs.q: What is the ‘essential religious practices’ test? Examine its strengths and weaknesses in deciding disputes over temples and festivals.
Should the State administer Hindu temples while mosques and churches are run by their communities? Discuss in the light of Article 26.

topics.t: Jammu and Kashmir: Statehood and security
topics.news: Three months of calm in J&K were broken in six days. A terror attack on a CRPF checkpoint in Kulgam on 11 November injured three jawans; a local suspected of joining the terror ranks was killed on 16 November after a six-day siege-like operation in Kulgam’s residential areas; and two Special Police Officers were found dead with bullet wounds in Kishtwar. Leaders have called the Kulgam operation ‘collective punishment’. It adds that the fall in attacks should not be mistaken for peace and asks the Centre to begin with restoring Statehood. Police say local recruitment into militancy in Kashmir is now in single digits.

blocks.h: Where J&K stands in the Constitution

rows: Art. 370 was read down on 5 August 2019. The **Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019** made J&K a Union Territory **with a legislature** and Ladakh a Union Territory without one, from 31 October 2019.

In the Article 370 reference a five-judge Bench upheld the abrogation, held that J&K had no internal sovereignty, and said Statehood should be restored at the earliest. The Centre had told the Court that Statehood would be restored.
The first Assembly elections in ten years were held in September–October 2024 and the National Conference government under Omar Abdullah took office in October 2024.
Under the 2019 Act the **Lieutenant Governor** controls police, public order and the All India Services. Note that the Chief Minister’s government has no jurisdiction over the police.
**Art. 3 and Art. 4** let Parliament form a State out of a Union Territory by an ordinary law passed by a simple majority. Such a law is not an amendment under Art. 368.
Puducherry (Art. 239A), Delhi (Art. 239AA) and J&K (under its own 2019 Act). Each has a different division of powers with the Centre.

ul: **Special Police Officers (SPOs):** temporary police volunteers paid an honorarium and used in counter-insurgency. In Nandini Sundar v. State of Chhattisgarh (2011) the Supreme Court held that using such poorly trained tribal youths as SPOs in anti-Naxal operations violated Arts. 14 and 21.
**The security view:** the ‘iron hand’ policy has cut terror attacks and local recruitment.

**The political view:** keeping whole villages under restrictions for days breeds alienation, as Mehbooba Mufti said of the Kulgam operation. The call is for security and political outreach to work together.
**Roadmap for Statehood:** a time-bound plan, as the Supreme Court and the Centre have both indicated.
**Proportionate operations:** limit restrictions on civilians, explain them in public, and have independent oversight of complaints.
**Talk to all stakeholders:** parties, civil society and local bodies, so that the 2024 voter turnout becomes trust in institutions.
**Be open about incidents:** the police and the Army have said little about how the two SPOs died, and conflicting reports spread.

prel.d: Lets Parliament form new States, change boundaries or names of States by law passed by a simple majority.
The law that created the Union Territory of J&K (with a legislature) and the Union Territory of Ladakh, from 31 October 2019.
Puducherry, Delhi and J&K; their elected Assemblies can legislate on some subjects, with the Centre and the Lieutenant Governor holding wide powers.
The Union government’s representative who administers a Union Territory; in J&K the post controls police and public order.
A temporary police volunteer, paid an honorarium, used mainly in counter-insurgency areas.
The Supreme Court judgment that upheld the abrogation of Article 370 and asked for the restoration of Statehood.
Punishing a whole community for what some of its members did; it is banned in international humanitarian law.

qs.q: Is the restoration of Statehood essential for lasting peace in Jammu and Kashmir? Examine with reference to the constitutional position after 2019.
qs.ref: 2025 GS2 (J&K Legislative Assembly after the 2019 Act)

qs.q: Distinguish between a State, a Union Territory with a legislature and one without. Why does the elected J&K government have limited powers over the police?
qs.ref: 2025 GS2 (J&K Legislative Assembly after the 2019 Act)

qs.q: Discuss the challenges of counter-insurgency operations in civilian areas and the safeguards needed to protect trust.

topics.t: The death penalty: ‘rarest of rare’ and the case for a moratorium
topics.news: India voted against a proposed global moratorium on the death penalty at the UN. It reports 574 people on death row on 31 December 2025, the highest since 2016. Per Project 39A the Supreme Court released 38 people from death row in 2016–2025 after about eight years there on average. India last carried out executions in 2020 (the Delhi gang-rape case), while the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita extended the list of capital offences. The ask is for a formal suspension of executions and a review of capital statutes.

rows: Art. 21 allows deprivation of life only by ‘procedure established by law’. Arts. 72 and 161 let the President and Governors grant pardon, remission or commutation.

Bachan Singh v. State of Punjab (1980) upheld the death penalty but only in the ‘rarest of rare’ cases after weighing aggravating and mitigating circumstances. Machhi Singh (1983) listed categories of such cases.
Mithu v. State of Punjab (1983) struck down Sec. 303 IPC that made death mandatory for a life convict who commits murder.
A sessions court’s death sentence has to be confirmed by the High Court before it can be carried out; the rule continues in the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023.
Shatrughan Chauhan v. Union of India (2014): unexplained and unreasonable delay in deciding a mercy petition is a ground to commute the sentence.
Swamy Shraddhananda (2008) and Union of India v. V. Sriharan (2015) let courts give life imprisonment for the rest of the convict’s life or a fixed term beyond 14 years instead of death.
The **262nd Report (2015, Justice A.P. Shah)** recommended abolishing the death penalty for all crimes except terrorism-related offences and waging war.

The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (in force from 1 July 2024) keeps death for murder and prescribes it for some new offences, such as a group of five or more killing on grounds of caste, race or community (mob lynching) and gang-rape of a girl under 18.

The General Assembly has passed a resolution for a moratorium on executions every two years since 2007. India has voted against, calling the death penalty a sovereign decision backed by judicial safeguards.

ul: **For retention:** retribution, deterrence and public confidence in cases of extreme violence.
**Against:** no evidence of added deterrence over life imprisonment (Law Commission, 2015); errors cannot be undone; unequal access to competent lawyers; and long years on death row.

**The asks:** suspend executions and review the capital statutes and the treatment of death-row prisoners; spare offences that do not involve intentional killing; strengthen investigation, prosecution and legal aid so that the system is fit for a punishment that needs near-infallibility.

prel.d: The test from Bachan Singh (1980): death is awarded only when life imprisonment is unquestionably foreclosed.
The power of the President and of the Governor to grant pardon, reprieve, remission or commutation of a sentence.
A National Law University Delhi project on the criminal justice system that publishes data on death-row prisoners.
The 2015 report that recommended abolishing capital punishment except for terrorism-related offences.
Replacing a sentence by a lighter one, such as death by life imprisonment.
A pause on carrying out death sentences, without removing the punishment from the law.
Using harsher punishment to answer public outrage without fixing policing or conviction rates.

qs.q: ‘The death penalty requires a near-infallible criminal justice system.’ Examine in the light of the ‘rarest of rare’ doctrine and the Law Commission’s views.
Should India join the global moratorium on the death penalty? Present arguments for and against.
What is the role of mercy petitions under Articles 72 and 161? How has the Supreme Court dealt with delay in deciding them?

topics.t: Mala fide: bad faith in State action (Azam Khan bail)
topics.news: The headline says a High Court granted interim bail to Azam Khan and held his arrest mala fide. Only the headline is available, so this note explains what mala fide means in law, how courts test it and the rules on arrest and bail.

rows: Bad faith: using a power for a purpose other than the one for which the law gave it, with a dishonest or improper motive, such as to harass a person. An action taken for such a purpose is a ‘colourable exercise of power’.
Malice in fact and malice in law
Malice in fact is actual ill-will or personal bias. Malice in law is an act done wrongfully, without just cause, even if no personal ill-will is shown.

The person alleging mala fides must prove it with clear and specific facts, since an official act is presumed to be done in good faith. Courts may draw the inference from circumstances, and the official accused should be made a party and heard.
E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) treated arbitrariness as the opposite of equality under Art. 14. The Court rejected the mala fides alleged on the facts but laid down this wider test.

Lord Diplock in the GCHQ case (1985) named illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety. ‘Wednesbury unreasonableness’ (1948) is the test of irrationality, and Indian courts also use proportionality.

Art. 22 gives the arrested person the right to be told the grounds and to be produced before a Magistrate within 24 hours. D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) laid down guidelines on arrest and custody, and Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014) said arrest should not be automatic for offences punishable up to seven years.

State of Rajasthan v. Balchand (1977) and Sanjay Chandra v. CBI (2012): bail is the rule and jail the exception, since pre-trial detention is not punishment. Interim bail is a temporary release while the application for regular or anticipatory bail is decided.
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 replaced the CrPC from 1 July 2024.

ul: **Where else mala fides arise:** transfers of officials, selective prosecution of political opponents, and laws said to be passed for a hidden purpose (colourable legislation).
**Why it matters:** the courts guard against the use of criminal law as a weapon in political rivalry, while still leaving investigation to the police.

prel.d: Done in bad faith, with an improper purpose.
Using a power for a purpose that the law did not give it, while pretending to use it for the proper one.
An act done wrongfully without just cause, even where no personal ill-will is shown.
A decision so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have made it; a ground of judicial review.
Temporary release from custody until the court decides the regular or anticipatory bail application.
The Supreme Court’s guidelines that police must not arrest automatically in offences punishable up to seven years.
Protection against arbitrary arrest and detention: grounds of arrest, a lawyer and production before a Magistrate within 24 hours.
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, which replaced the Code of Criminal Procedure from 1 July 2024.

qs.q: What is mala fide action in administrative law? How do courts prove and deal with it?
qs.ref: 2017 GS4 (RTI case study on public accountability)

qs.q: ‘Bail is the rule and jail the exception.’ Discuss the balance between personal liberty and the needs of investigation.
How can the law prevent the misuse of arrest powers for political purposes?

topics.t: India–ASEAN, East Asia Summit and the Quad in Manila
topics.news: At the 23rd India–ASEAN Summit in Manila, PM Modi said the world needs peace and predictability. East Asia Summit members issued a joint declaration on tackling cybercrime, as many online-fraud cases originate in Southeast Asia, and India will host a summit on it at the National Forensic Sciences University in Gandhinagar and an East Asia Summit University Heads Conclave at Nalanda. The Quad leaders then met for the first time since 2024, and the first time since the US–Israel attacks on Iran and the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz began over nine months ago (at least 23 Indians, mainly seafarers, have died in that war). They opposed unilateral changes to the status quo by force or coercion and economic coercion such as arbitrary export restrictions, and launched a Quad Business Forum to be held in Mumbai. Mr Trump said he would meet Mr Putin and Mr Xi at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, the first three-way ‘G-3’ summit.

rows: Formed in 1967 by the Bangkok Declaration; Timor-Leste became the 11th member in October 2025. The Philippines chairs ASEAN in 2026. Headquarters: Jakarta. The ASEAN Charter (2008) made it a legal entity.

Sectoral partner 1992, full dialogue partner 1996, summit-level partner 2002 and strategic partner 2012. The ASEAN–India Trade in Goods Agreement (signed 2009, in force 2010) is under review. The **Act East Policy (2014)** upgraded the Look East Policy of 1991.

Started in 2005 as the leaders’ forum on strategic issues in the region, led by ASEAN. Members are the ASEAN states plus India, China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand and, since 2011, the United States and Russia.

India, the US, Japan and Australia. First formed in 2007, revived in 2017; leaders’ summits since 2021 (Washington 2021, Tokyo 2022, Wilmington 2024). Work areas: a free and open Indo-Pacific, maritime domain awareness (IPMDA), supply chains, technology and health.
Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation: 21 economies, founded in 1989. India is not a member.

Scam compounds in Myanmar, Cambodia and Laos have trafficked and defrauded many Indians. The UN General Assembly adopted a Convention against Cybercrime in December 2024; India is not a party to the Budapest Convention.

ul: **Why export controls matter to India:** China recently restricted critical minerals and heavy equipment such as tunnel-boring machines, which hurts Indian infrastructure work.
**Why the Gulf matters:** India imports most of its crude oil and a large share of its gas by sea, and Hormuz is the passage for much of it.
**ASEAN centrality:** India backs ASEAN’s role in the Indo-Pacific, while building the Quad as a flexible group that does not replace it.

prel.d: Association of Southeast Asian Nations, formed in 1967; it now has 11 members.
India’s 2014 policy of deeper economic, strategic and cultural links with the Asia-Pacific, upgrading the 1991 Look East Policy.
An ASEAN-led annual leaders’ forum on regional strategic issues that began in 2005.
The grouping of India, the US, Japan and Australia for a free and open Indo-Pacific.
Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness; a Quad plan to track activity at sea with shared data.
Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a forum of 21 economies; India is not a member.
ASEAN–India Trade in Goods Agreement, in force since 2010.
The label used for a possible three-way summit of the US, China and Russia.

qs.q: ‘The Quad is moving from a security grouping to a wider partnership.’ Discuss with reference to its recent summit and India’s interests.
qs.ref: 2020 GS2 (Quad as a trade bloc) · 2026 GS2 (IPMDA)

qs.q: How has India’s Act East Policy deepened ties with ASEAN? Identify the challenges.
qs.ref: 2026 GS1 (shift of trade to the Indo-Pacific)

qs.q: Examine the threat of cross-border cyber-fraud networks and the need for regional cooperation.

topics.t: Microfinance and the RBI: inclusion without over-indebtedness
topics.news: RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu stressed that financial inclusion must not come at the cost of household over-indebtedness and that responsible lending begins before a loan is sanctioned. After two years of contraction the sector looks steadier. Early-stage delinquency (30–179 days overdue) fell to 1.9% in June 2026 from 6.1% a year before, but loans overdue by more than 180 days were still 17.4%. The SIDBI–Equifax report puts the outstanding portfolio at ₹2.69 lakh crore, down 12%, with 7.15 crore active loan accounts, while disbursements in April–June 2026 rose 17% to ₹62,302 crore.

rows: Small loans, savings and insurance for households that banks do not reach, delivered by NBFC-MFIs, banks, small finance banks, Self-Help Groups (the NABARD SHG–Bank Linkage Programme began in 1992) and Joint Liability Groups.
A non-deposit-taking NBFC with at least 75% of its net assets in qualifying microfinance loans. The Malegam Committee (2011), set up after the Andhra Pradesh crisis of 2010, led to this category.

One common definition for all regulated lenders: household annual income up to ₹3 lakh, and total loan repayments not above **50% of household income (FOIR)**. The earlier interest-rate cap was removed and lenders must have a board-approved pricing policy.
Raise the ₹3 lakh income limit (set in 2022) for wages and inflation, and review the uniform 50% FOIR, with some repayments assessed on interest alone.

Leaving out the principal would understate indebtedness. A study it cites found the average borrower spends 18.7% of monthly household income on repayment. Flexibility will depend on better income assessment, credit reporting and responsible lending.

A standard sheet in simple language of the loan’s all-in cost, charges and recovery process; mandatory for retail and MSME loans since October 2024. The Deputy Governor wants it explained in the borrower’s own language.

A borrower signs without understanding what is in the document. The Deputy Governor contrasted it with ‘mindful consent’ and warned it could spread to digital loans, instant personal loans and credit cards.

MFIN and Sa-Dhan are the RBI-recognised self-regulatory organisations, but their members are the lenders they oversee. Lenders may also sell insurance and other products, which can clash with the borrower’s needs.
RBI’s June 2026 directions on the advertising, marketing and sale of financial products ban deceptive practices and require explicit consent; they take effect from 1 January 2027.

ul: **Why the sector matters:** it reaches women entrepreneurs, informal workers and rural households. It contributed about 2% of GVA in 2018–19 and is projected at 2.7% by 2025–26.
**The risk:** when crude oil, transport and food prices squeeze income, extra credit can turn into distress. Borrowers pushed out of the regulated system may turn to moneylenders.
**Way forward:** assess repayment capacity household by household, share data across credit bureaus, train field staff, and put an independent check on self-regulation.

prel.d: A non-banking finance company that lends mainly small loans to low-income households and does not take deposits.
NABARD’s programme, begun in 1992, of lending to Self-Help Groups through banks.
Fixed obligation to income ratio: the share of household income that goes into loan repayments; capped at 50% in the 2022 framework.
A one-page, plain-language statement of the cost and terms of a loan.
Signing a loan paper without understanding it.
Self-regulatory organisation: an industry body that sets and enforces rules for its members under the regulator’s recognition.
Having debt repayments that are too high for a household’s income.
Loans overdue by 30 to 179 days.

qs.q: Is financial inclusion possible without over-indebtedness? Examine the RBI’s approach to microfinance.
Discuss the role and limits of Self-Help Groups and microfinance institutions in poverty reduction.
What is ‘pseudo-consent’ in lending? Suggest measures to protect borrowers in the age of digital credit.

topics.t: States’ spending on cash transfers
topics.news: The report ‘State of State Finances 2026-27’ says States’ spending on subsidies and transfers rose from 16% of their revenue receipts in 2018-19 to 21% in 2023-24. States are estimated to spend about 1% of GDP (about ₹4 lakh crore) together on cash transfer schemes in 2026-27, up from 0.6% in 2022-23.

rows: Revenue receipts are tax and non-tax income. Spending on cash transfers is **revenue expenditure** that creates no asset, unlike capital expenditure on roads, schools and irrigation.

The Finance Commission (Art. 280) recommends how Union taxes are shared; the 15th Commission gave States 41% of the divisible pool. Art. 293 limits State borrowing, and each State has its own FRBM law that caps the fiscal deficit (usually at 3% of GSDP).
DBT (2013) sends money to a bank account, using the JAM trinity of Jan Dhan, Aadhaar and mobile. It cuts leakage, which is why States prefer cash to subsidised goods.

S. Subramaniam Balaji v. State of Tamil Nadu (2013) held that manifesto promises of freebies are not a ‘corrupt practice’, and asked the Election Commission to frame guidelines. In 2022 the matter of freebies was referred to a larger Bench, where it remains.
RBI’s State Finances: A Study of Budgets tracks States’ deficits, debt, revenue and the quality of spending.

ul: **In favour:** income support to women and the poor, higher consumption, local demand and women’s control over spending.
**Against:** less room for capital spending that raises growth; spending that is hard to cut; pressure on FRBM limits; and borrowing outside the budget to meet the bills.
**Way forward:** target the transfer, publish its cost and the way it is financed, link some of it to outcomes such as schooling or health, and keep capital spending protected.

prel.d: Tax and non-tax income of a government, excluding borrowing and asset sales.
Spending that does not create an asset, such as salaries, subsidies and cash transfers.
Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management: laws that set deficit and debt targets; States have their own.
Gross State Domestic Product.
Direct Benefit Transfer; payment of benefits straight to bank accounts.
Limits the borrowing powers of States.
Free goods or services, or cash, promised by parties to voters; the Supreme Court has referred the legal questions to a larger Bench.

qs.q: Examine the trend of State spending on cash transfers and its implications for fiscal federalism and capital expenditure.
Is the distinction between welfare and ‘freebies’ meaningful? Discuss the role of courts and the Election Commission.
What reforms can help States balance welfare spending with fiscal discipline?

topics.t: Wheat sowing and the rise in horticulture output
topics.news: Wheat, the main rabi crop, has been sown on 50.07 lakh hectares so far, down 15.27% from 59.10 lakh hectares a year ago, according to the Agriculture Ministry. Separately, the third advance estimates put India’s horticulture output in 2025-26 at 3,869.15 lakh tonnes, up 4.36% (161.77 lakh tonnes) from 3,707.38 lakh tonnes in 2024-25, even though the area under horticulture fell. Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said farmers were moving beyond traditional crops to fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices, plantation crops (cashew, coconut, cocoa) and aromatic and medicinal plants.

rows: Sown in October–December and harvested in March–April. Main crops: wheat, barley, gram, peas and mustard. They need cool weather while growing and warm, dry weather while ripening.

The second major cereal after rice. It is grown mostly in the northern plains (Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Bihar) under irrigation. A heat wave in March, when the grain fills, can cut yields.
The Cabinet fixes the Minimum Support Price on the advice of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) before the sowing season.
Sowing continues till December, so early-season gaps often narrow. Delays come from a late paddy harvest, soil moisture and the supply of fertiliser and seed.
India is the second-largest producer of fruits and vegetables after China, and leads in mango, banana and papaya. Horticulture output has exceeded foodgrain output since 2012-13.
The Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture (2014) is a centrally sponsored scheme for growth of the sector. The National Horticulture Board (1984) supports post-harvest and market work.

The Golden Revolution (1991–2003) pushed horticulture. Operation Greens (2018) steadies prices of tomato, onion and potato. The Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (2020, ₹1 lakh crore) funds cold storage and processing.
Why output rose on less land
The Minister pointed to this as the key feature of the estimates: higher yields through better varieties, protected cultivation and drip irrigation.

ul: **Significance:** higher income per hectare, nutrition, exports, jobs in processing and cold chains.
**Challenges:** perishability, weak cold chains, price swings (the TOP crops), small holdings and climate stress.
**The data point to watch:** advance estimates are revised later as final data come in.

prel.d: A crop sown in winter (October–December) and harvested in spring (March–April), such as wheat and mustard.
Minimum Support Price at which the Government is ready to buy a crop.
Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices, which recommends MSPs.
Mission for Integrated Development of Horticulture, a centrally sponsored scheme started in 2014.
The period (1991–2003) of rapid growth in horticulture, honey and related sectors.
A 2018 scheme to stabilise prices of tomato, onion and potato.
Early official estimates of area and production, revised as more data arrive.

qs.q: Discuss the shift in Indian agriculture from foodgrains to horticulture. What policy support is needed?
How do weather and sowing patterns in the rabi season affect wheat output and prices?
What are the challenges in the horticulture value chain, and how can they be addressed?

topics.t: Artificial intelligence and official statistics (VISTAR)
topics.news: AI and Machine Learning are core pillars of the newly approved Viksit Bharat Initiative for Statistical Transformation, Analytics & Research (VISTAR), meant to overhaul India’s official data. A warning: synthetic data, which AI generates, could slip into official estimates and be mistaken for evidence. VISTAR also proposes raising the number of major surveys from 43 to 59 during the 16th Finance Commission cycle.

rows: The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) and its National Statistical Office (NSO). The National Statistical Commission (2005) advises on standards, and the Collection of Statistics Act, 2008 governs collection.
PLFS (employment), the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey, and the Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises (ASUSE, 2025: over 6.7 lakh establishments in 24,153 first-stage units).
Artificial data produced by statistical models or AI (such as GANs) that copies the patterns of real data without copying the observations. Legitimate uses: privacy, testing algorithms, scarce data.

It inherits the gaps of the data it learns from, such as under-counted informal work, unpaid work by women and farm distress. It can miss local shocks, so a district estimate may look complete but fail to show a closed factory or seasonal migration. The WEF (2025) also warns of ‘model collapse’ and a ‘liar’s dividend’ that erodes trust in even real data.
Funds for schemes such as the rural job guarantee (VB-G RAM G) or cash transfers could be misallocated if district numbers rest on modelled households.
A large share of activity is outside formal accounts. Moves such as an MDR on UPI could push more payments into cash, leaving fewer digital traces.

The UNECE 2025 Framework on Responsible AI for Official Statistics stresses fairness, accountability, transparency and validity. The UN Fundamental Principles of Official Statistics (1994) require independence and professional standards.

The Gauss–Markov theorem: under its assumptions, ordinary least squares gives the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator. Not every problem meets these conditions, but the aim is the same: unbiased, reliable estimates backed by evidence.

ul: **Way forward:** keep primary surveys as the bedrock; label model estimates separately from survey estimates; have human oversight, ground checks and an audit trail; and protect the independence of official statistics.

prel.d: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, which runs the NSO and official surveys.
Viksit Bharat Initiative for Statistical Transformation, Analytics & Research; an overhaul of India’s official data system using AI and ML.
Artificially generated data that mimics real data patterns.
Generative Adversarial Network: an AI model that learns patterns from data and generates new, similar records.
The decline in quality of AI models trained repeatedly on AI-made data.
Periodic Labour Force Survey, the main source of employment data.
Annual Survey of Unincorporated Sector Enterprises.
Best Linear Unbiased Estimator, the Gauss–Markov result for ordinary least squares.

qs.q: Can AI-generated estimates replace field surveys in official statistics? Discuss the benefits and risks.
Why is the credibility of official data important for policy and welfare delivery? How can it be protected?
What are the data challenges of measuring India’s informal economy?

topics.t: Transgender rights: the 2026 Amendment and the SIR deletions
topics.news: Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026 earlier this year. It removes self-identification: a person now needs a medical board’s recommendation, a choice from prescribed categories and a District Magistrate’s certificate. A Hindu data analysis says the transgender electorate in the States and Union Territories covered by the Special Intensive Revision fell 31.4%, from 45,610 to 31,300, below even the 2019 level. Delhi’s draft rolls lost nearly 64% and Tamil Nadu about 10%. On the national portal 48,707 people had registered for the certificate by November, with over 9,000 applications pending.

rows: Recognised a ‘third gender’ and the right of every person to self-identify gender under Arts. 14, 15, 16, 19(1)(a) and 21, and asked for reservation as a socially and educationally backward class.

Bars discrimination in education, jobs, healthcare and access to public goods. A certificate of identity was issued by the District Magistrate on the person’s application, and a changed male or female certificate needed proof of surgery. It set up a National Council for Transgender Persons and a Complaints Officer in each establishment.
Read down Sec. 377 IPC for consenting adults and treated sexual orientation as part of dignity and privacy.
The right to privacy under Art. 21 includes identity and bodily autonomy.

Replaces self-identification with a medical board’s recommendation, a selection from prescribed categories (socio-cultural identities such as kinner, hijra, aravani, jogta and persons with specified variations in sex characteristics) and DM certification, with no appeal or independent review. Trans men, trans women and genderqueer persons fall outside the definition.
WHO’s ICD-11 moved gender incongruence out of the chapter on mental disorders. The WPATH Standards of Care, version 8 (2022), support gender-affirming care.
It flags gaps in education, healthcare, property, employment, documentation and policing and urges self-identification and independent grievance redress.

ul: **Why the voter numbers matter:** Art. 326 gives universal adult suffrage. The ECI first recorded transgender electors under ‘Others’ in 2009, and the category grew after NALSA. Enrolment nearly doubled from 28,046 (2014) to 45,610 (2024). Turnout among enrolled transgender voters rose from 7.8% to 27%. Census 2011 counted roughly 4.8 lakh transgender persons.
**Why they are deleted more easily:** migration after family rejection, no documents, and a certificate that is harder to obtain.

**Health care:** medico-legal hurdles delay or stop care, push people to unregulated sources and add to distress. The Madras High Court’s Sushma ruling (2021) asked for training of health staff on transgender health. The Centre’s SMILE scheme (2022) supports livelihood and shelter, including Garima Greh shelter homes.
**Autonomy vs protection:** should the State protect by medical and administrative gatekeeping or by maximising autonomy with safeguards against exploitation?
**Welfare and identity are different questions:** the Act conflates legal recognition of gender identity with eligibility for benefits.
**Suggestions:** treat transgender health as part of general healthcare, train staff, allow a preferred name and identity in records, and set up the Complaints Officers the 2019 Act requires.

prel.d: The Supreme Court judgment that recognised the third gender and the right to self-identified gender.
The principle that a person’s gender identity is what the person declares, without a medical or other test.
The law that bars discrimination against transgender persons and provides identity certificates and a National Council.
Shelter homes for transgender persons under the SMILE scheme of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment.
Support for Marginalised Individuals for Livelihood and Enterprise; a 2022 scheme for transgender persons and for persons engaged in begging.
The World Health Organization’s 11th International Classification of Diseases; it no longer treats gender incongruence as a mental disorder.
Elections to the Lok Sabha and Assemblies are held on adult suffrage.
A Madras High Court judgment with directions on the rights and healthcare of LGBTQIA+ persons, including training of staff.

qs.q: ‘Recognition of gender identity should rest on autonomy and dignity, not on medical certification.’ Examine in the light of the NALSA judgment and the 2026 Amendment.
qs.ref: 2026 GS2 (right to privacy relating to self-identity)

qs.q: How can the electoral rolls be made inclusive for transgender persons and other marginalised groups during a mass revision?
qs.ref: 2026 GS2 (right to privacy relating to self-identity)

qs.q: Discuss the social, legal and health challenges faced by transgender persons in India and the steps needed to mainstream their healthcare.

topics.t: Fake drugs: facts, law and regulation
topics.news: Dinesh S. Thakur says reports that fake cancer drugs were seized from a licensed distributor in Karnataka are unconfirmed: the State has not confirmed it, and the list that circulated on social media held only antibiotics. He cites the National Drug Survey (2017), which found only 0.0245% of drugs counterfeit, and urges a response in proportion to the problem. He also asks for a licensing framework for people who transport drugs and for Good Distribution Practices.

rows: The **Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940** and its Rules. It treats adulterated, spurious, misbranded and ‘not of standard quality’ drugs as separate categories. The 2008 amendment raised penalties and set up special courts.

The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) under the Drugs Controller General of India approves new drugs and sets standards. State licensing authorities license manufacture and sale, and Central Drugs Laboratories test samples.
A seller who proves that he bought the drug from a licensed source under a written warranty and stored it properly is protected. This is why records of every purchase matter.

The National Drug Survey found 0.0245% of the drugs counterfeit, far from the ‘25%’ figure once attributed to the WHO in the press. The author says the real risk is low because drug trading has legal record-keeping and so is a poor target for counterfeiters.

Since 2023 QR or bar codes are required on the labels of the top 300 drug brands (Schedule H2). The author warns that costly mandatory technology raises drug prices and that anti-counterfeiting solution providers lobby for it.
Revised Schedule M (December 2023) tightened Good Manufacturing Practices; larger firms had to comply first, small units later.

No licensing framework for those who transport drugs between manufacturers, distributors and retailers (raised by the Supreme Court in the 1970s). The adoption of WHO’s Good Distribution Practices has been pending for over a decade.

ul: **The wider point:** a headline about fake cancer drugs causes fear among patients. If the seizure is real, the State should name the drugs and hospitals; if not, it should say so.
**Quality scares abroad:** contaminated cough syrups were linked to child deaths in The Gambia and Uzbekistan in 2022, which led India to tighten testing of ingredients.
**Way forward:** proportionate rules, a licence for drug transport, Good Distribution Practices, strong State drug labs and more inspectors.

prel.d: A drug that imitates another or is sold under another maker’s name.
A drug that fails the quality tests but is not a fake.
Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, India’s national drug regulator.
Drugs Controller General of India; heads the CDSCO.
The main law on import, manufacture, sale and distribution of drugs and cosmetics.
The part of the Drugs Rules that sets Good Manufacturing Practices.
WHO guidance on proper storage and transport of medicines.
A code to trace a drug through the supply chain; mandatory for the top 300 brands since 2023.

qs.q: Discuss the regulatory framework for ensuring the quality of medicines in India. What are its gaps?
How should policy respond to the threat of counterfeit drugs without raising the price of medicines?
Examine the role of the media and the State in communicating health risks responsibly.

topics.t: Malaria in India: progress and the road to elimination
topics.news: President Droupadi Murmu inaugurated the golden jubilee of the ICMR–National Institute of Malaria Research (ICMR-NIMR). She said malaria cases and deaths fell by nearly 80% between 2015 and 2025, high-burden districts fell from 155 to 33, and 160 districts reported zero indigenous malaria cases in 2022–2025. She noted India’s exit from the WHO’s High Burden to High Impact group in 2024, and welcomed the indigenous malaria vaccine being developed in Bhubaneswar.

blocks.h: Malaria: the disease and the response

rows: Caused by Plasmodium parasites (P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. malariae, P. ovale and P. knowlesi) and spread by the bite of female Anopheles mosquitoes. P. falciparum is the deadliest; P. vivax is widespread in India and can relapse.
ICMR-NIMR, Delhi, studies the parasite, mosquito vectors, vector control, insecticide resistance and community surveillance. It also works on the urban malaria vector Anopheles stephensi.
The National Framework for Malaria Elimination (2016–2030) aims at elimination by 2030. The National Strategic Plan for 2023–27 is run by the National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control.
The ‘High Burden to High Impact’ approach (2018) targets countries with the most malaria cases and deaths. India left the group in 2024 as its burden fell.

Rapid diagnostic tests; artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) for falciparum; chloroquine and primaquine for vivax; long-lasting insecticidal nets; indoor residual spraying; larvivorous fish (Gambusia); and clearing breeding sites.
WHO has recommended two vaccines for children: RTS,S/AS01 (2021) and R21/Matrix-M (2023). The Indian vaccine being developed in Bhubaneswar (at an ICMR regional centre) is indigenous.
The WHO certifies countries as malaria-free: the Maldives (2015), Sri Lanka (2016), China (2021), and Cabo Verde and Egypt (2024).
World Malaria Day is on 25 April. World Mosquito Day (20 August) marks Ronald Ross’s 1897 discovery in Secunderabad of the parasite in the mosquito; he won the Nobel Prize in 1902.

ul: **What the President asked for:** better diagnosis, treatment and surveillance; mosquito control; new medicines and vaccines; public awareness and community participation; and research results that reach villages.

**The remaining challenges:** drug and insecticide resistance, urban malaria, malaria in forested and tribal areas, migration across borders, and climate change that lengthens the transmission season.

prel.d: The genus of parasites that cause malaria.
The genus of mosquitoes that spread malaria; only the female bites.
Artemisinin-based combination therapy; the standard treatment for falciparum malaria.
Long-lasting insecticidal net.
High Burden to High Impact; a WHO-backed approach for the countries with the most malaria.
National Framework for Malaria Elimination, 2016–2030.
The two malaria vaccines recommended by the WHO for children.
ICMR’s National Institute of Malaria Research in Delhi.

qs.q: Evaluate India’s progress against malaria and the strategies needed to eliminate it by 2030.
How can research institutions like ICMR-NIMR help in controlling vector-borne diseases in a changing climate?
Why does malaria persist in tribal and forested areas? Suggest community-based measures.

topics.t: Community Study Centres for tribal students in Keralam
topics.news: A Hindu article describes Samoohya Patana Muri, the Community Study Centres (CSCs) begun by the Keralam government in 2018 for children from tribal communities. The authors argue that Indian education policy counts enrolment, buildings, equipment and pass rates (access) but not whether students feel able to take part, ask for help and keep going after failure. A study of 462 tribal students in Kasaragod found that those who rated their CSC positively had stronger achievement motivation and better social skills.

blocks.h: What the centres do and what they show

rows: Run by the Scheduled Tribes Development Department for ST and SC students of Classes V to XII: tutoring, learning materials and light refreshments (₹20 per student a day). Every centre employs an educated young person from the local community. There were 364 CSCs, per the Economic Review 2023.

Positive views of the centre went with higher motivation and social skills. The authors say the point is not that tribal children lack social skills. Their communities value cooperation, while schools reward competition, and the centre helps students to cope.
The better a CSC works, the easier it is for the school to stay unchanged. Schools must also adapt to the students they serve.

Art. 21A (free and compulsory education from 6 to 14 years) and the RTE Act, 2009; Art. 46 (promote the educational and economic interests of SCs and STs); Art. 15(4) (special provisions); Art. 275(1) (grants for tribal welfare); Art. 338A (National Commission for Scheduled Tribes).

Eklavya Model Residential Schools (since 1997–98), pre- and post-matric scholarships, PM JANMAN (2023) for particularly vulnerable tribal groups, and the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (2024).
Teaching in the mother tongue in the early years and special attention to socio-economically disadvantaged groups (SEDGs).

ul: **What to measure:** whether students freely seek help, feel respected, and progress to higher levels without liberal moderation or grace marks, not just attendance and pass rates.
**Treat the facilitator as an educator:** train in adolescent development, learning strategies and counselling, and pay regularly.
**Peer tutoring:** let senior students support younger ones in mixed-age projects. None of this replaces computers and learning materials.

prel.d: Community Study Centres of the Keralam government for tribal students.
A Directive Principle that asks the State to promote the education and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections.
Grants-in-aid from the Union to States for tribal welfare and Scheduled Area administration.
Eklavya Model Residential Schools for tribal students.
Socio-economically disadvantaged groups, a category in NEP 2020.
Access means enrolment and facilities; participation means students are active and confident in learning.
The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes.

qs.q: Does India’s tribal development policy reflect a socially grounded and equity-based approach? Justify your answer.
‘Access alone does not ensure achievement.’ Discuss with reference to education of tribal children.
Examine the role of community-based learning centres in improving educational outcomes of marginalised groups.

topics.t: A space-security doctrine for India
topics.news: A defence analyst argues that India needs a comprehensive space-security doctrine. Satellites underpin communications, navigation, weather forecasting, banking and the armed forces, and the threat has moved from destroying satellites to disrupting their services through jamming, spoofing, cyber interference and electronic warfare, where attribution is hard. He asks for clear thresholds, attribution standards and response principles, built on resilience, space-domain awareness, quick recovery and coordination with commercial operators, without pushing the weaponisation of space.

rows: Space is free for exploration, no nation can claim it, weapons of mass destruction cannot be placed in orbit, and States are responsible for national space activity, including by private firms. India is a party.
The Liability Convention (1972) makes a launching State liable for damage caused by its space object. The Registration Convention (1975) requires objects to be registered.
India’s anti-satellite test. A DRDO interceptor hit a satellite in low-Earth orbit at about 300 km.
The Defence Space Agency (2019, Bengaluru) and the Defence Space Research Organisation.
ISRO focuses on research and advanced missions, IN-SPACe authorises and promotes private activity as a single window, and NewSpace India Limited is the commercial arm.
ISRO’s annual Indian Space Situational Awareness Report (ISSAR-2025) covers tracking, collision avoidance and debris reduction. IS4OM and the NETRA project support it.

Jamming (blocking signals), spoofing (false signals, for example to navigation receivers), cyber attacks on satellite networks and ground stations, and electronic warfare. They can disable a service without damaging the spacecraft.
A collision cascade in orbit (the Kessler syndrome) could make orbits unusable. ISRO aims for debris-free space missions by 2030.

ul: **The questions to ask:** is destroying a satellite different from jamming it? How is blame assigned when interference comes through a network of actors? How to tell an accident from an attack? How to respond without escalating when attribution is unclear?
**Why industry must be included:** commercial operators now run much of the communications and navigation that public services use, so security depends on the whole ecosystem.

**What the doctrine should do:** deter, withstand, attribute and recover, while keeping outer space for peaceful use. Its measure should be preserving function and recovering fast, not the number of capabilities.

prel.d: The basic treaty of space law: free use, no national appropriation, no weapons of mass destruction in orbit.
India’s 2019 anti-satellite missile test at about 300 km altitude.
Anti-satellite weapon.
Blocking a signal, and sending false signals to mislead a receiver.
Knowing what objects and events are in orbit and near one’s satellites.
A chain of collisions that creates so much debris that orbits become unusable.
The tri-service agency, set up in 2019, that runs the military’s space capabilities.
The authority that authorises and promotes private space activity in India.

qs.q: Space has become a part of national critical infrastructure. Discuss the changing threats to space assets and the need for a space-security doctrine for India.
Examine the international legal framework governing outer space. Does it address new threats such as jamming and cyber interference?
How can private space companies contribute to national security? What risks do they raise?

topics.t: India–Japan 2+2, JAIMEX and the Indian Navy’s exercises and ships
topics.news: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh visits Japan on 18–19 November for the fourth India–Japan Foreign and Defence Ministers’ Dialogue (2+2) in Tokyo, co-chaired with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, with Japan’s Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi. It will be his third meeting with Mr Koizumi this year, and the focus is defence cooperation, maritime security and defence industry. INS Sahyadri took part in the bilateral maritime exercise JAIMEX 2026 with the Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force on 13–14 November, alongside the JMSDF ship JS Ise, with tactical manoeuvres, communication drills and cross-deck landings.

rows: Special Strategic and Global Partnership (2014). The 2+2 dialogue began in 2019. An Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement (2020) lets the two forces use each other’s supplies and facilities.
INS Sahyadri is a Shivalik-class (Project 17) stealth frigate built at Mazagon Dock and commissioned in 2012. JS Ise is a Hyuga-class helicopter destroyer of the JMSDF.
JIMEX/JAIMEX (navies; JIMEX began in 2012), Dharma Guardian (armies) and Shinyuu Maitri (air forces). Japan is also a permanent partner in Malabar and a member of the Quad.
Both look to a free and open Indo-Pacific. Japan is India’s partner in the Mumbai–Ahmedabad high-speed rail project and in defence technology talks.
US, Japan, Australia: the Quad navies. Began as an India–US exercise in 1992; Japan a permanent member since 2015 and Australia since 2020. Malabar 2024 was hosted off Visakhapatnam.
India, Brazil and South Africa; first held in 2008.
Zayed Talwar, Al Mohed Al Hindi, Naseem Al Bahr
Africa–India Key Maritime Engagement: India with African navies.
A multilateral gathering of navies hosted by the Eastern Naval Command at Visakhapatnam, since 1995.
The US-led exercise off Hawaii; India has taken part since 2014.
Coordinated patrols with Thailand, Indonesia and Bangladesh, and short passage exercises with visiting foreign ships.

blocks.h: Indian Navy: carriers, ships and submarines

rows: **INS Vikramaditya** (ex-Admiral Gorshkov, bought from Russia, commissioned 2013) and **INS Vikrant** (the first indigenous carrier, built by Cochin Shipyard, commissioned on 2 September 2022, about 45,000 tonnes). Earlier carriers: INS Vikrant (1961–97, formerly HMS Hercules) and INS Viraat (1987–2017, formerly HMS Hermes). A third carrier has been discussed, but not sanctioned. The Navy has ordered 26 Rafale-M fighters for its carriers.
Delhi class (Delhi, Mysore, Mumbai); Kolkata class (Kolkata, Kochi, Chennai; Project 15A); Visakhapatnam class (Visakhapatnam, Mormugao, Imphal, Surat; Project 15B).

Shivalik class (Shivalik, Satpura, Sahyadri); Talwar class (six ships built in Russia); Brahmaputra class; and the **Nilgiri class (Project 17A)** of seven ships, whose lead ship INS Nilgiri was commissioned in January 2025 and Himgiri and Udaygiri together on 26 August 2025.

Kamorta-class anti-submarine corvettes (Kamorta, Kadmatt, Kiltan, Kavaratti), Kora, Khukri and Veer classes, Mahe-class anti-submarine shallow-water craft (INS Arnala, 2025), offshore patrol vessels and survey vessels.
Deepak-class fleet tankers and the amphibious transport dock INS Jalashwa (formerly USS Trenton).

Nuclear ballistic-missile submarines INS Arihant (2016) and INS Arighaat (2024), with more of the class under construction; Kalvari-class (Scorpène, Project 75) diesel-electric boats; Sindhughosh (Kilo) and Shishumar classes.

Western Naval Command (Mumbai), Eastern (Visakhapatnam) and Southern (Kochi, training). The Andaman and Nicobar Command (Port Blair, 2001) is the first tri-service command. Karwar (Project Seabird) is the largest naval base on the west coast.

ul: **INS Vikrant (1961–97) in 1971:** the old Vikrant took part in the naval blockade of East Pakistan during the Bangladesh Liberation War.

prel.d: A meeting of the foreign and defence ministers of two countries.
Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force.
The India–Japan bilateral maritime exercise; the older series is JIMEX.
A pact that lets two armed forces use each other’s supplies, services and facilities.
The naval exercise of the Quad countries: India, the US, Japan and Australia.
A multinational naval gathering hosted by India at Visakhapatnam since 1995.
The Nilgiri-class stealth frigate programme of seven ships.
India’s first indigenous aircraft carrier, commissioned in 2022.
India’s Scorpène-design diesel-electric submarines built under Project 75.

qs.q: Examine the significance of the India–Japan 2+2 dialogue and maritime exercises for the Indo-Pacific.
Discuss the role of the Navy’s bilateral and multilateral exercises in India’s maritime strategy.
Assess the progress of indigenisation in naval shipbuilding, with examples of carriers, frigates and submarines.

topics.t: Cyclone Akvan and the Bay of Bengal
topics.news: Cyclonic storm Akvan, centred about 590 km east of Chennai at 5.30 p.m. on Tuesday, moved slowly and is now expected to become a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal on Wednesday morning and a very severe cyclonic storm by Thursday. Landfall is likely between Visakhapatnam and Nellore, with winds of 100–110 km/h along the coast from Wednesday evening and heavy rain in the northern Andhra districts. The IMD Director General called it a rare event that all of this year’s three or four Bay of Bengal cyclones are crossing near Andhra Pradesh, last seen in 1987, and linked it to El Niño.

blocks.h: How cyclones form, are graded and named

rows: Sea surface above about 26.5°C to a depth of about 50 m, humid air, low vertical wind shear, a pre-existing disturbance and a Coriolis force strong enough to spin the system (more than about 5° from the equator).

Depression 31–49 km/h; deep depression 50–61; cyclonic storm 62–88; severe cyclonic storm 89–117; very severe cyclonic storm 118–165; extremely severe cyclonic storm 166–220; super cyclonic storm 221 km/h or more.
IMD is the Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre for the north Indian Ocean, in New Delhi, issuing advisories for the 13 countries of the WMO/ESCAP Panel on Tropical Cyclones.

Names are used in sequence from a list of 169 proposed by the 13 Panel countries in 2020. In this sequence Arnab (Bangladesh) and Murasu (India) were followed by **Akvan (proposed by Iran)**. The scheme started in 2004.
Two cyclone seasons: pre-monsoon (April–June) and post-monsoon (October–December). The Bay of Bengal sees several times more cyclones than the Arabian Sea.
Four stages: pre-cyclone watch, cyclone alert, cyclone warning and post-landfall outlook, with colour codes green, yellow, orange and red.

blocks.h: Why the east coast is exposed and how India prepares

ul: **Exposure:** a funnel-shaped bay and wide continental shelf raise the storm surge, and the low-lying deltas of the Mahanadi, Godavari and Krishna are densely settled.
**El Niño link:** the IMD chief tied this year’s unusual pattern, with every cyclone crossing near Andhra Pradesh, to El Niño. A similar run last occurred in 1987.

**Institutions:** the National Disaster Management Authority (Disaster Management Act, 2005), the National Disaster Response Force and the State authorities. The National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project builds shelters, embankments and warning systems.
**The Odisha record:** deaths fell from about 10,000 in the 1999 Super Cyclone to double digits in Phailin (2013) and Fani (2019), thanks to early warning, mass evacuation and shelters.

prel.d: A storm with maximum sustained winds of 62–88 km/h on the IMD scale.
A cyclone with sustained winds of 118–165 km/h.
IMD’s Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre for tropical cyclones over the north Indian Ocean.
The rise in sea level that a cyclone drives onto the coast; the main cause of death.
The effect of Earth’s rotation that spins a cyclone; it is absent at the equator.
A warming of the central-eastern Pacific that changes weather around the world.
National Cyclone Risk Mitigation Project: shelters, embankments and early warning on India’s coast.
The point where the centre of a cyclone crosses the coast.

qs.q: Why does the Bay of Bengal produce more tropical cyclones than the Arabian Sea, and why does the east coast suffer more? Discuss the measures that have reduced casualties.
qs.ref: 2014 GS1 (where tropical cyclones are confined) · 2024 GS1 (sea surface temperature)

qs.q: Explain the meaning of the colour-coded warnings and the stages of cyclone warning issued by IMD.
‘Community participation is the cornerstone of effective disaster management.’ Analyse with examples from India’s cyclone management.

topics.t: Assam: national parks, rare animals and human–elephant conflict
topics.news: The headline reports clashes during an elephant rescue mission in Assam; the full story is not available, so this note gives the background on Assam’s protected areas, its rare and listed animals and the human–elephant conflict.

rows: On the Brahmaputra floodplain in central Assam. UNESCO World Heritage Site (1985) and tiger reserve (2006). Home to the largest population of the greater one-horned rhinoceros (2,613 in the 2022 census), with tigers, elephants, wild water buffalo, swamp deer and the Bengal florican.
On the Bhutan border. UNESCO World Heritage Site (1985), Project Tiger reserve (1973) and Biosphere Reserve (1989). Golden langur, pygmy hog, hispid hare, wild water buffalo and Bengal florican.
On the north bank of the Brahmaputra, sometimes called the ‘mini Kaziranga’ for its rhinos; a tiger reserve since 2016.
In Sonitpur on the Jia Bhoroli river, next to Pakke in Arunachal Pradesh. A tiger reserve with elephants and the white-winged wood duck.
In Tinsukia and Dibrugarh. Biosphere Reserve (1997) and national park (1999) with a famous population of feral horses and the white-winged wood duck.

Both became national parks in 2021. Raimona (Kokrajhar) shelters the golden langur. Dehing Patkai, a lowland rainforest called the ‘Amazon of the East’, is known for its wild cats and an elephant reserve.

Pobitora (the highest density of one-horned rhinos), Hoollongapar (India’s only gibbon sanctuary), Chakrashila (golden langur), Deepor Beel (a Ramsar site near Guwahati) and Majuli, a very large river island.
IUCN Vulnerable; Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Assam’s state animal. The Indian Rhino Vision 2020 translocated rhinos to Manas. World Rhino Day is 22 September.
IUCN Endangered; Schedule I; National Heritage Animal (2010); Project Elephant began in 1992. Assam has five notified elephant reserves, including Kaziranga–Karbi Anglong and Dehing Patkai.
IUCN Endangered; found in Kaziranga, Manas, Nameri and Orang.
IUCN Critically Endangered, the world’s smallest wild pig; Manas, with captive breeding under the Pygmy Hog Conservation Programme (1996).
IUCN Critically Endangered grassland bird; Kaziranga, Manas and Dibru-Saikhowa.
IUCN Endangered primate found only in western Assam and Bhutan; Chakrashila, Manas and Raimona.
IUCN Endangered; India’s only ape; Hoollongapar.
IUCN Endangered; the National Aquatic Animal (2009); the Brahmaputra and its tributaries.
IUCN Endangered; the state bird of Assam (Deo Hans).
A globally threatened stork nesting around Guwahati; the community-led ‘Hargila Army’ protects it.
IUCN Endangered rabbit of the tall grasslands of Manas.

ul: **Causes:** loss and breaking up of forest by roads, railways, tea estates and encroachment, narrowing corridors and crop-raiding.

**Law and policy:** killing an elephant is punishable under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Project Elephant (1992) protects habitat and corridors, and 101 elephant corridors have been identified in the country.
**What helps:** safe corridors, early-warning fences and alerts, rapid rescue teams, quick compensation, and involving villagers in conservation.

prel.d: UNESCO World Heritage Site in Assam, famed for the one-horned rhino.
A national park, tiger reserve, biosphere reserve and World Heritage Site on the Assam–Bhutan border.
The 1973 programme to protect the tiger and its habitat through reserves.
The 1992 central scheme to protect elephants, their habitats and corridors.
The list of the most protected species under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
A Critically Endangered pig, the smallest wild pig, found in Assam’s grasslands.
India’s only ape, found in the north-east.
A strip of land that connects elephant habitats and lets herds move safely.
A women’s group in Assam that protects the greater adjutant stork (hargila).

qs.q: Discuss the factors responsible for human–elephant conflict in India and suggest solutions.
Assam’s protected areas are important for the survival of many Critically Endangered and Endangered species. Discuss.
How do corridors and community participation help conservation in the Brahmaputra valley?

topics.t: The 2026 Earthshot Prize in Mumbai
topics.news: The 2026 Earthshot Prize awards were held in India for the first time, in Mumbai. Britain’s Prince William said Gen Z are ‘torchbearers’ of global change. The five winners were Mahindra Last Mile Mobility (Clean Our Air), Niue Ocean Wide Trust (Revive Our Oceans), Bhutan (Protect and Restore Nature), PFAS-Free France (Build a Waste-Free World) and Ørsted (Fix Our Climate).

rows: Founded in 2020 by Prince William and the Royal Foundation. Five £1 million prizes each year until 2030, in five categories: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. The first awards were in 2021.
Clean Our Air: electric three-wheelers on India’s roads. Policy link: FAME (2015) and PM E-DRIVE (2024) support electric vehicles.
Revive Our Oceans: protecting the ocean, especially in the Pacific. Niue is a self-governing State in free association with New Zealand.

Protect and Restore Nature: protection of Himalayan forests that feed the water systems of about 1.6 billion people downstream. The Constitution (Art. 5) requires at least 60% of land to stay under forest at all times.
Build a Waste-Free World: a national cross-party movement to ban ‘forever chemicals’ in consumer products and make polluters pay for cleaning up.
Fix Our Climate: a Danish energy company that moved from coal-heavy power to renewable energy.

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances. They do not break down in nature and are used in non-stick cookware, firefighting foam and water-proof fabrics. The Stockholm Convention has listed PFOS (2009), PFOA (2019) and PFHxS (2022).

ul: **Indian finalists:** Mahindra Last Mile Mobility won, and the Mahila Housing Trust (linked to SEWA, Ahmedabad) was also among this year’s finalists.
**Prince William’s message:** young people are not waiting for a solution; India shows that progress cannot wait in spite of heavy environmental pressure.

prel.d: A prize for solutions to the world’s environmental problems, with five £1 million awards each year until 2030.
‘Forever chemicals’ that do not break down in nature.

topics.t: Renewable energy: corporate investment and India’s clean-power push
topics.news: Amazon said it will invest a further $7 billion in renewable energy in India by 2030, in addition to the $4 billion it has already contracted.

rows: 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070 (the ‘Panchamrit’ pledges at COP26, 2021). The updated NDC (2022) promises 50% of installed electric capacity from non-fossil sources by 2030 and a 45% cut in emission intensity of GDP from 2005. India reached the 50% non-fossil capacity mark in 2025.

PM-KUSUM (2019) for solar pumps and farm feeders; **PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (2024)** for rooftop solar for one crore households; the National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023); production-linked incentives for solar modules; solar parks and Green Energy Corridors.

Companies buy clean power through power purchase agreements and Green Energy Open Access Rules (2022), and meet obligations with renewable energy certificates. Data centres are driving up electricity demand.

Ministry of New and Renewable Energy; Solar Energy Corporation of India (2011); IREDA; the Central Electricity Authority; the International Solar Alliance (launched in Paris in 2015, headquartered in Gurugram).
The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023) under the Energy Conservation Act sets up a market for emission reductions.

Intermittency and the need for storage (batteries and pumped hydro); transmission limits and curtailment; land; dependence on imported solar cells and raw materials (the ALMM list pushes domestic modules and cells); and the weak finances of power distribution companies.

ul: **Why companies invest:** to cut their own emissions, hedge power prices and meet buyers’ climate targets. Whether new projects add to India’s capacity, rather than only re-assigning existing power, is the test of real impact.
**Way forward:** pair solar and wind with storage, build grids ahead of generation, give open access to buyers, and support domestic manufacturing.

prel.d: India’s five pledges at COP26 (2021), including 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070.
Nationally Determined Contribution: a country’s climate pledge under the Paris Agreement.

The right of large consumers to buy renewable power directly from a producer.
Solar Energy Corporation of India, set up in 2011.
International Solar Alliance, launched in 2015, headquartered in Gurugram.
Switching off renewable generation because the grid cannot take it.

topics.t: Biogas and sustainable aviation fuel
topics.news: Reliance Industries plans about 100 compressed biogas (CBG) plants by 2030, costing about ₹15,000 crore ($1.6 billion), to produce about 5 million cubic metres a day from agricultural residue. It runs 45 plants now, below capacity, and plans 10 more by March 2027. Separately, Indian Oil has government approval to supply sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) commercially from its Panipat refinery, enough for the 1% blending target for international flights in 2027, and will sign airline supply agreements before investing in more SAF projects.

rows: Biogas purified to more than 90% methane, made from farm residue, cattle dung, sugarcane press mud and municipal waste. It can replace CNG and piped gas, and the leftover slurry is a fertiliser.
SATAT (Sustainable Alternative Towards Affordable Transportation, October 2018) set up a market for CBG. GOBARdhan (2018) turns cattle dung and farm waste into biogas and organic manure.
It can cut stubble burning, capture methane that would escape, reduce imports of gas and add rural income.

Sustainable aviation fuel: jet fuel made from non-fossil feedstock such as used cooking oil or agricultural residue, with a lower life-cycle carbon footprint. It can be blended with ordinary aviation fuel (up to 50% is allowed under the standard). India’s indicative targets are 1% for international flights in 2027, 2% in 2028 and 5% in 2030.
The International Civil Aviation Organization’s scheme to offset growth in international aviation emissions above the 2020 level.
The National Policy on Biofuels (2018, amended in 2022) aimed at 20% ethanol blending, which India reached in 2025. The JI-VAN Yojana (2019) supports second-generation ethanol.

ul: **Demand-led approach:** Indian Oil will first sign airline supply agreements and only then commit more money, so production follows demand.
**Open questions:** assured supply of feedstock, price premium over ordinary aviation fuel, and the cost for airlines. Cheap collection of farm residue is the key for biogas.

prel.d: Compressed biogas: purified biogas with over 90% methane, usable as a fuel.
A 2018 scheme to build CBG plants and create a market for them.
A 2018 scheme to turn cattle dung and farm waste into biogas and manure.
Sustainable aviation fuel, a low-carbon substitute for jet fuel.
Aviation turbine fuel, the usual jet fuel.
ICAO’s scheme to offset international aviation emissions above the 2020 level.
Petrol blended with 20% ethanol.
Burning of crop residue after harvest, a major cause of winter air pollution in north India.

topics.t: Science in brief: IN-SPACe city maps, Voyager 1 and the Top500
topics.news: IN-SPACe selected three firms, SpacePixxel Technologies, KaleidEO Space Systems and Azista Industries, to build High-Resolution Indian Human Settlement Layers from satellite images, with seed funding of ₹1.46 crore. Voyager 1 is one light-day from Earth today, almost 26 billion km away at 61,000 km/h. China’s LineShine kept the top place in the Top500 list of supercomputers released at SC26, becoming the first machine above 2 quintillion calculations a second (2.198 quintillion, using about 42 MW). India’s highest-ranked machine is Shakti Cloud at No. 35.

rows: The Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre (2020) is a single-window regulator and promoter within the Department of Space, based in Ahmedabad. NewSpace India Limited (2019) is ISRO’s commercial arm.

Funded under the Seed Fund Scheme for Use Case Demonstration by Non-Government Entities. The firms will use single (monocular) satellite images to produce three outputs: built-up surface and building type, building height and built-up volume.
NITI Aayog asked for accurate and detailed data on human settlement for urban planning, infrastructure, disaster-risk assessment and population estimates.
National Geospatial Policy (2022) and the SVAMITVA scheme, which maps rural habitation land with drones.

Launched by NASA on 5 September 1977 (Voyager 2 on 20 August 1977). It crossed the heliopause in 2012 and is the farthest and the oldest operating space mission, but only two of its ten science instruments remain online.
About 26 billion km: a radio signal takes a full day each way.

The ultraviolet spectrometer, built for ultraviolet light, was found to be picking up galactic cosmic rays. At Saturn, signals through the rings revealed gaps and structures, and signals through Titan’s atmosphere gave its temperature and pressure. These fed into the Cassini–Huygens mission.

In 1990, researchers used Voyager 1 data at Saturn to confirm to 1% accuracy that radiation changes frequency in a gravitational field. Gravity Probe A (1976) had done so to 0.02% accuracy, but the Voyager result was independent.
The boundary of the region dominated by the Sun’s solar wind, beyond which lies interstellar space.
A list, published twice a year (June and November), that ranks the fastest supercomputers by the LINPACK benchmark.

Built by the Shenzhen Cloud Computing Centre and installed at the National Supercomputing Centre in Shenzhen. It runs on China-made processors and the Kylin operating system and was built for atmospheric and ocean research. It first topped the list in June 2026, displacing the US El Capitan.
The top ten were unchanged from June, with only 27 newcomers (a record low) as the entry level rose by 7.3%. The next machines are El Capitan, Frontier and Aurora (US) and JUPITER Booster (Germany).

The National Supercomputing Mission (2015), run by MeitY and the Department of Science and Technology through C-DAC and IISc, aims at a network of supercomputers across institutions. PARAM Siddhi-AI is one of its machines.

ul: **Why it matters:** supercomputers power weather and climate models, drug research and defence simulations, and the US limits on advanced chips to China make a Chinese-built, Chinese-chip machine at the top a notable signal.

prel.d: The authority that promotes and authorises private-sector space activity in India.
Map layers that show built-up areas, building heights and volumes from satellite data.
The boundary of the Sun’s solar wind, the start of interstellar space.
The distance light travels in a day, about 26 billion km.
High-energy particles that reach the solar system from outside it.
The biannual list that ranks the world’s most powerful supercomputers.
A machine that can do a quintillion (10 to the power 18) calculations a second.
A 2015 mission to build a national network of supercomputers.
